rules.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, inscne
rules.text: Most nouns in the fifth declension are feminine.

rules.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, deireadh an ainmnigh uatha
rules.text: Fifth-declension nouns end in -in, -il, -ir or in a vowel in the nominative singular (traein, abhainn, riail, triail, cathaoir, litir, uimhir, lacha, cara, comharsa).

rules.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, deireadh an ghinidigh uatha
rules.text: In the genitive singular these nouns end in -ch, -n, -d or -r, which gives four main groups of nouns; Nollaig (genitive Nollag) is treated separately as a fifth group.

rules.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra
rules.text: Most fifth-declension nouns form their plural in -(e)acha (traenacha, litreacha, cathaoireacha, mainistreacha, aithreacha); a small number are irregular and must be learned: bráithre, caoirigh, ingne, lachain, cairde, monarchana, comharsana, naimhde, nollaigí, tríochaidí.

rules.point: an ginideach uatha ar -(e)ach
rules.text: Group A nouns add -(e)ach in the genitive singular: an chathaoir becomes na cathaoireach, an litir becomes na litreach, an eochair becomes na heochrach. Some drop a vowel (syncopate) before the ending: an chathair becomes na cathrach, an mhainistir becomes na mainistreach.

rules.point: an ginideach uatha ar -n
rules.text: Group B nouns end in -n in the genitive singular: an abhainn becomes na habhann, an chomharsa becomes na comharsan, an teorainn becomes na teorann, an mhonarcha becomes na monarchan, an ionga becomes na hiongan, an lacha becomes na lachan.

rules.point: an ginideach uatha ar -d
rules.text: Group C: cara ends in -d in the genitive singular, an cara becomes an charad (teach an charad).

rules.point: an ginideach uatha ar -r
rules.text: Group D, the family words, end in -r in the genitive singular and drop the i of the last syllable: an t-athair becomes an athar, an deartháir becomes an dearthár, an bráthair becomes an bhráthar, an mháthair becomes na máthar, and an deirfiúr becomes na deirféar.

rules.point: an ginideach uatha, Nollaig
rules.text: Group E: Nollaig has the genitive singular Nollag, tús na Nollag.

rules.point: an ginideach iolra
rules.text: For nouns whose plural ends in -(e)acha or -e the genitive plural is the same as the nominative plural, with eclipsis after na (dath na gcathaoireacha, troime na n-eochracha, tithe na gcairde); but caoirigh, comharsana and lachain take the short genitive plural caorach, comharsan, lachan (cosa na gcaorach, gairdíní na gcomharsan, cleití na lachan).

rules.point: an ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha
rules.text: A noun that follows a verbal noun goes into the genitive: ag casadh na heochrach, ag glanadh na monarchan.

rules.point: réamhfhocail chomhshuite agus an tuiseal ginideach
rules.text: A compound preposition (a simple preposition plus a noun, such as ar son, i measc, os comhair) is followed by the genitive case: the noun after it goes into the genitive, and the article becomes an (masculine), na (feminine) or na (plural) with the usual genitive mutations. Ulster usage is the same as the standard here: the lenition that Ulster uses after a simple preposition and the article (ar an bhord) does not apply after a compound preposition, because the noun is in the genitive (ar son an bhoird, ar son na tíre).

rules.point: na réamhfhocail chomhshuite is coitianta
rules.text: Each of these takes the genitive. All of them are used in Ulster; pupils will also hear fá choinne (for, to get) beside le haghaidh, and it takes the genitive in the same way.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha le 'ag' (Tá sé ag canadh)
rules.text: The verbal noun is used after 'ag' with the verb 'bí' to say what someone is doing now: Tá sé ag canadh, Tá sí ag scuabadh, Tá siad ag obair. Pages 178 to 181 teach this through photograph captions only. The question that goes with it in Ulster is 'Cad é atá ar siúl aige?' rather than 'Céard atá ar siúl aige?'.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -adh/-eadh
rules.text: Most one-syllable (first conjugation) verbs form the verbal noun by adding -adh after a broad ending and -eadh after a slender ending: dún, dúnadh; glan, glanadh; bris, briseadh; scaip, scaipeadh.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -t
rules.text: Verbs ending in a slender consonant such as -n, -l or -r add -t to form the verbal noun: bain, baint; tiomáin, tiomáint; oscail, oscailt; freagair, freagairt; imir, imirt.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -ú/-iú
rules.text: Most second conjugation verbs in -aigh or -igh drop that ending and take -ú (broad) or -iú (slender): gortaigh, gortú; ceartaigh, ceartú; cruinnigh, cruinniú; bailigh, bailiú.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -ach/-each
rules.text: A small group of -aigh/-igh verbs take -ach or -each instead of -ú/-iú: ceannaigh, ceannach; réitigh, réiteach; cuardaigh, cuardach; fuadaigh, fuadach; clúdaigh, clúdach.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, leathnú an chonsain deiridh
rules.text: Some verbs form the verbal noun by broadening the final consonant, with no ending added: cuir, cur; siúil, siúl; iompair, iompar; ceangail, ceangal; freastail, freastal.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, briathra neamhrialta
rules.text: The irregular verbs have their own verbal nouns which must be learned: abair, rá; beir, breith; bí, bheith; feic, feiceáil; ith, ithe; faigh, fáil; tar, teacht; téigh, dul; clois, cloisteáil; tabhair, tabhairt; déan, déanamh. In Ulster the verb 'cluin' (verbal noun cluinstin) is commonly used for 'clois', and 'tchí mé' is the present tense of 'feic', but the verbal noun stays 'feiceáil'.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, slite éagsúla eile
rules.text: Other verbs form the verbal noun in various individual ways (-áil, -eacht, -amh, -ean, -int, -í, -ím, -íocht): nigh, ní; fág, fágáil; éirigh, éirí; lig, ligean; imigh, imeacht; cónaigh, cónaí; caith, caitheamh; seas, seasamh; dúisigh, dúiseacht; léigh, léamh; rothaigh, rothaíocht; tit, titim; inis, insint.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha gan athrú
rules.text: Some verbs do not change at all: the verbal noun is the same as the root, including most verbs in -áil (cniotáil, bácáil, sábháil, spáráil, tástáil, pacáil, iarnáil) and others such as díol, goid, fás, léim, rith, snámh, scríobh, troid, úsáid, obair, foghlaim, stad, gáire, ól, and in Ulster amharc.

rules.point: bí leis an ainm briathartha (an aimsir láithreach agus an aimsir ghnáthláithreach)
rules.text: The verb 'bí' is very often used with the verbal noun, for example Bíonn sé ag obair go crua. In Ulster the present forms are tá mé, tá tú, tá sé/sí, tá muid, tá sibh, tá siad (negative níl mé, níl muid; question an bhfuil mé, an bhfuil muid) and the habitual present forms are bím, bíonn tú, bíonn sé/sí, bíonn muid, bíonn sibh, bíonn siad (negative ní bhím, ní bhíonn muid; question an mbím, an mbíonn muid). The first person singular keeps its own ending (bím). The impersonal forms táthar, níltear, bítear, ní bhítear are as in the standard.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, a cumadh
rules.text: Ulster forms the verbal adjective exactly as the standard does.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -ta
rules.text: Broad roots ending in l, n, s, ch and similar sounds take -ta: dall becomes dallta, dún becomes dúnta, múch becomes múchta.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -te
rules.text: Slender roots take -te: bris becomes briste, mill becomes millte, roinn becomes roinnte. A root ending in slender -igh drops the -igh before -te: léigh becomes léite, pléigh becomes pléite, suigh becomes suite.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -tha
rules.text: Broad roots ending in b, c, d, g, m, p or r take -tha: cíor becomes cíortha, crom becomes cromtha, fág becomes fágtha, scuab becomes scuabtha, leag becomes leagtha.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, na foircinn -aithe agus -ithe
rules.text: Second-conjugation verbs ending in -aigh or -igh replace that ending with -aithe (broad) or -ithe (slender): críochnaigh becomes críochnaithe, ceannaigh becomes ceannaithe, deisigh becomes deisithe, imigh becomes imithe.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -fa
rules.text: Roots ending in -bh or -mh replace that ending with -fa: scríobh becomes scríofa, treabh becomes treafa, lobh becomes lofa.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha le tá agus ag
rules.text: The verbal adjective is used with tá to describe a completed state (Tá an doras dúnta), and with ag plus a pronoun to say who has done the action (Tá an féar bainte agam). In Ulster the same pattern is used; where a noun follows ag and the article, lenite it: Tá an pháirc treafa ag an fheirmeoir.
